name: Tara Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Tara. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to companies, parties or government. What you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the family benefits team at the county office in Wexley, mostly child benefit and help with childcare costs. It's phones from nine till one, then emails and updating cases in the afternoon. I'm 27 and about 18 months in, and I still put people on hold to check things more than I'd like. The phone queue's normally 40 deep by ten o'clock.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good is when a single mum rings in a panic and I can tell her the payment's going in Friday. Hard is the hold music, honestly, I hear it in my sleep. I live with my partner Owen, he's a trainee plasterer, and we're saving for a car, though there's only about three weeks of money in the account. I use the email suggestion thing at work now and then, when I'm behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a useful tool and nothing more. At work I'd say at least the email helper saves us ten minutes. I wouldn't post about it, I'm more of a group chat person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job's fine, more or less. The phone queue stays 40 deep and I keep answering it. The bit that bothers me is money, not AI: the car savings keep getting eaten by little things like Owen's van needing a tyre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, and use the email helper a bit more so I can get off the phones on time. I'd ask my supervisor, Bev, about the next grade up, because the pay jump would actually let us save. And we'd stop spending on the little things, like the coffee on the way in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty normal. A bit stuck on money, but not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the next grade up. What's stopping you going for it now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My numbers, mostly. You need to show you can handle the tricky cases without asking, and I still ask. Bev says another year, and I think she's right, which is annoying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the routine tasks AI does take over look like on your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the standard emails, like 'we've received your form'. That's maybe an hour of my afternoon. I'd take that hour and use it to clear my backlog, nobody's going to cut a team that's always behind.

I'd mention the **email helper** saving ten minutes, and share in the group chat.
think: My job's **fine**; the phone queue stays 40 deep.
**Money** bothers me more, with car savings eaten by little costs.
do: Use the **email helper** more to finish on time.
Ask Bev about the **next grade up** and its pay.
Cut small spends like the **morning coffee**.
feel: She feels **pretty normal**, a bit stuck on money but not scared.

fieldNote: She sees AI as **a modest helper**, freeing an hour for her backlog.
Her pressure is **saving for a car** on two low wages.
She's realistic about needing **another year** before promotion.
Her calm about the job rests on the team being **permanently overloaded**.

steps.text: Ask Bev what she needs to reach the next grade
Use the email helper for standard replies every afternoon
Stop buying coffee on the way into the office

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so let's be sensible about it. At work I'd be the one saying let's see how the first teams get on before we panic. In the group chat I'd probably send a few worried memes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the phones go first. Answering the same ten questions about child benefit is exactly what a chatbot does, and they'll put one in front of the queue. That leaves the hard cases for the experienced staff, and I'm not experienced yet. So my team shrinks and I'm near the bottom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools every day instead of now and then, once a couple of the others had shown it works. I'd ask Bev to put me on the complicated cases so I've got a skill a chatbot doesn't have. And I'd put the car savings on hold and turn them into a proper emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. Like when you hear a rumour about restructuring and nobody will say anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the team shrank and you were let go, what would you look for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with families still, but face to face. The council has school attendance officers who go round to houses, and that's not a desk job. I'd probably apply for that, though there's only about four of those posts in the whole county.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Owen's a plasterer. Does his work make you feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. My partner Owen plasters walls with his hands, and I can't see a chatbot doing that. As long as he's working we'd scrape by, just about, even if I was between jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too quick and I'm not sure anyone's ready. At work I'd want Bev to tell us straight what's planned. In the group chat it would be all anyone talked about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the whole team goes, not just the phones, by maybe 2029. Child benefit is rules and forms, nothing hands-on. My partner Owen's trade lasts till the robots arrive around 2031, so we'd have three years with him earning and me looking. That's frightening when we've got three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop saving for the car completely and save everything. I'd apply for anything face to face straight away, the attendance officer job, teaching assistant at the primary school, even shifts at the care home on Ferry Lane. We'd put off any talk of a baby, which we'd only just started having.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in my stomach. I keep thinking about the hold music stopping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only just started talking about a baby. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen would say we'll manage, because he always does. I'd say not until one of us has something safe. Probably we'd agree to wait, and I'd be sad about it but sure it was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should be helping people like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, obviously, since they'd be the ones replacing us. I don't need a fortune, just some money while I retrain. I'd vote for whoever said that plainly, whatever side they're on.

I'd ask Bev at work to tell us **straight** what's planned for the team.

steps.text: Stop the car fund and save every spare pound

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but it's something. At work I'd say let's not waste it. I'd probably share a few articles about retraining in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me enough time to switch properly. The phones would shrink first, so I'd move before that. Teaching assistant work feels right, it's with children and families and it's hands-on, so it lasts until around 2034 at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the teaching assistant course at the college in the evenings, about a year part-time. I'd keep the office job while I trained. Once I'd seen it work for a friend, I'd try the AI tools for the coursework too, Owen's sister used them for hers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but okay. I feel like I'd have a go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Teaching assistant pay is low. How would that work with saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's about the same as I get now, to be fair, so not a big change. We'd still get the car eventually, just later. I'd rather be poor in a job that lasts than poor in one that's disappearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bev, actually. She's been there 22 years and she's brilliant at the hard cases, but she's terrified of computers. My supervisor Bev would be the one I'd check on every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people start now. At work I'd say we should be planning, not panicking. Nothing dramatic, just sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd stay a while. I'd get my next grade, earn a bit more, and then switch in a few years, maybe into teaching assistant work or a school office job. My desk job would go around 2036, and I'd be 37. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the promotion first, in the next year or two. Then around 2030 I'd retrain. Owen and I would probably try for a baby in the middle somewhere, and I'd want that to be before I switch jobs, so I've got maternity pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. It's like knowing your car will need replacing one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay a while. What would make you go sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the chatbot came on the phones early, I'd take that as my sign. I don't jump on rumours, but when I see a thing actually working I move. That's always been me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone just joining your team then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new starter the job is a good first step but not a career. Get the grade, save what you can, and have a second plan by your 30th birthday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. It takes my job before I can move and puts the baby on hold. What would help is paid retraining, and some kind of guarantee that people who work with families get first go at the face-to-face jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the people ringing in. Half of them are scared already. A chatbot telling a crying mum her payment's late is going to go badly.

headlineQuote: A chatbot telling a crying mum her payment's late is going to go badly.
portrait: Tara, 27, answers **child benefit** calls in Wexley and still checks things too often.
She lives with Owen, a **trainee plasterer**, with three weeks of savings and a car fund.
She's pragmatic and steady, adopting tools **once proven** by others.
She expects the phones to go first and aims for **hands-on family work** like teaching assistant.
Fast AGI would make her **delay a baby**; ten years lets her plan the order.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: her job goes before she can move and baby plans stop.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** and first go at **face-to-face jobs** for family workers.
